topic.title: The Framework Behind a 75-Unit Portfolio: How Aaron Murphy Replaced His Income in 11 Years

loan_encouragement.reason: This is a case study in general real estate investing mechanics—house hacking, BRRRR, vertical integration, and scaling a rental portfolio—that illustrate replicable concepts any residential investor could apply. However, the article itself is a profile/interview rather than market or product data, so connecting these principles to actual loan products or timing requires scripting work beyond what the source material directly supports.

selectedHook.hook: You're waiting for a six-figure salary before you start investing. Aaron Murphy ran the numbers on a $30,000 salary and found real estate was the only path that worked mathematically.
selectedHook.rationale: This hook directly confronts the viewer's most likely barrier to action (perceived need for high income) with a named, quantified fact (Aaron's actual $30,000 salary analysis) that proves the assumption wrong. It's psychologically the most disruptive because it invalidates the excuse most viewers tell themselves, making them want to see how he actually did it. The other hooks are strong but rely on explaining pivots or unusual tactics; this one targets the core hesitation keeping people from starting at all.

workingTitle: The Math Behind Building a 75-Unit Portfolio on a Starting Salary

beats.line: Aaron Murphy's first mortgage was $2,000 a month.
You're waiting for a six-figure salary before you start investing. Aaron Murphy ran the numbers on a $30,000 salary and found real estate was the only path that worked mathematically.
He started with a house hack in 2016—put down $11,900 on his first property and rented out four rooms at $700 each.
His second deal: a $96,000 triplex. He put down 20%—about $19,000.
Then another $20,000 in renovations to get three units rented.
Total monthly rent across those three units: $1,900.
A cash-out refi on that triplex pulled $50,000—which became half the seed for scaling into BRRRR deals.
On a typical BRRRR, he buys for $100K, puts in $30-$40K in renovations, adds $20K in closing costs both ends. All in: $150-$160K.

The real lesson: starting capital and leverage, not income level, determine whether a real estate strategy can work. Low down payments and forced appreciation through renovation let small starting amounts compound into portfolios.
Aaron's path is documented: 2016 start, 75 units by 2027—built through sequential BRRRR deals, each one refinanced to fund the next without waiting for six-figure income.
$11,900 down on the first deal. $50,000 pulled from one refi to scale. No six-figure paycheck required.
